title: Anywhere in the Field, and Columns

scenes.tts: Take a simple cell's best bar and slide it sideways, off the on strip and onto an off strip. What happens to the sum?
scenes.caption: Take a simple cell's best bar and slide it sideways, off the ON strip and onto an OFF strip. What happens to the sum?
scenes.visual: The simple-cell grid with its meter. A bright bar sits on the green ON strip. On-screen text: Slide the bar sideways. What does one sum do?
scenes.narration: Take a simple cell's best bar and slide it sideways, off the ON strip and onto an OFF strip. What happens to the sum?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: It falls past zero and goes negative. This cell goes from firing hard to falling silent.
scenes.visual: The bar slides one column to the side. The meter swings from +6 down to −3 (shown on screen); the raster runs, then stops.
scenes.narration: It falls past zero and goes negative. This cell goes from firing hard to falling silent.

scenes.tts: Hubel and Wiesel's complex cells did. A correctly oriented bar drove them over much of the field.
scenes.visual: A second field, plain grey with no strips, labelled complex cell. The same bar slides across it; its raster keeps running through most positions, strongest near the middle and fading near the edges. Label: relative position tolerance.
scenes.narration: Hubel and Wiesel's complex cells did. A correctly oriented bar drove them over much of the field.

scenes.tts: A bar at the wrong angle still did little. In many complex cells that answered spots, turning a spot on and turning it off excited the same places, unlike a simple cell's separate on and off subregions. Other complex cells did not answer small spots.
scenes.caption: A bar at the wrong angle still did little. In many complex cells that answered spots, turning a spot on and turning it off excited the same places, unlike a simple cell's separate ON and OFF subregions. Other complex cells did not answer small spots.
scenes.visual: The bar turns to the wrong angle over the complex-cell field; the raster goes sparse. Small spots flash on and off at the same places; both onset and offset make the raster tick, and no green or magenta marks form. Small label: example of overlapping ON and OFF responses, not every complex cell.
scenes.narration: A bar at the wrong angle still did little. In many complex cells that answered spots, turning a spot on and turning it off excited the same places, unlike a simple cell's separate ON and OFF subregions. Other complex cells did not answer small spots.

scenes.tts: One sum cannot do that. Swap a bright bar for a dark one, and the sum flips sign.
scenes.visual: Back on the simple-cell grid: a bright bar on the ON strip shows +6; it turns dark and the meter shows −6. Label: reverse the contrast, flip the sign.
scenes.narration: One sum cannot do that. Swap a bright bar for a dark one, and the sum flips sign.

scenes.tts: Their proposal applies the rule twice. Several simple cells share one angle, with fields at slightly different places.
scenes.visual: Three simple-cell fields with the same vertical strips, offset side by side.
scenes.narration: Their proposal applies the rule twice. Several simple cells share one angle, with fields at slightly different places.

scenes.tts: All of them excite one complex cell. Where their responses overlap enough, at least one of them answers as the bar shifts.
scenes.visual: Arrows from the three simple cells converge on one complex cell. A shaded band marks the covered excitatory region, the span of the three ON strips, narrower than the outlines of the three full fields. The bar slides across the band; at each position one simple cell lights and the complex cell keeps firing, its response weakening near the band's edges and stopping when the bar reaches the outer OFF margins.
scenes.narration: All of them excite one complex cell. Where their responses overlap enough, at least one of them answers as the bar shifts.

scenes.tts: So the complex cell keeps its preferred angle and gains tolerance of position.
scenes.visual: Label under the complex cell: keeps orientation, tolerates position.
scenes.narration: So the complex cell keeps its preferred angle and gains tolerance of position.

scenes.tts: This second step is still debated. Some complex cells receive direct geniculate input, and circuits within cortex contribute.
scenes.visual: A dashed arrow runs from an LGN cell straight to the complex cell, labelled direct input. Small loops inside cortex are labelled intracortical circuits. A tag reads: still debated.
scenes.narration: This second step is still debated. Some complex cells receive direct geniculate input, and circuits within cortex contribute.

scenes.tts: In cat and monkey, an electrode going straight down through cortex meets cells that tend to share an angle. That is a column.
scenes.visual: An electrode descends at right angles to the surface. Each cell it passes shows a small bar, all at nearly the same angle. Label: column.
scenes.narration: In cat and monkey, an electrode going straight down through cortex meets cells that tend to share an angle. That is a column.

scenes.tts: Does a cell need neighbours that agree with it in order to be tuned?
scenes.visual: On-screen text: Does tuning need neighbours that agree?
scenes.narration: Does a cell need neighbours that agree with it in order to be tuned?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: No. Imaging rat visual cortex cell by cell found sharply tuned cells. Their neighbours preferred unrelated angles.
scenes.visual: A top-down sheet of cells, each coloured by its preferred angle. For cat, orderly patches of colour. For rat, a speckled mix of colours. Labels: cat; rat.
scenes.narration: No. Imaging rat visual cortex cell by cell found sharply tuned cells. Their neighbours preferred unrelated angles.

scenes.tts: This layout is called salt and pepper. Tuning does not need a map.
scenes.caption: This layout is called salt-and-pepper. Tuning does not need a map.
scenes.visual: The rat sheet enlarges. Label: salt-and-pepper. Caption: tuning does not need a map.
scenes.narration: This layout is called salt-and-pepper. Tuning does not need a map.

scenes.tts: So tuning does not need neighbours that agree. How each cell gets its preference is a separate question.
scenes.visual: One rat cell is circled; its own tuning curve appears beside it, with neighbours preferring other angles. Small label: how each cell is tuned is not shown by this experiment.
scenes.narration: So tuning does not need neighbours that agree. How each cell gets its preference is a separate question.

scenes.tts: So keep the rule and its limit. A simple cell adds up the light in its field, and the field's layout largely sets its preference. A complex cell needs more than one sum.
scenes.visual: Caption card: Simple cell: one sum; layout largely sets preference. Complex cell: more than one sum.
scenes.narration: So keep the rule and its limit. A simple cell adds up the light in its field, and the field's layout largely sets its preference. A complex cell needs more than one sum.
